reason: I fetched both presentations and the two sentences are verbatim in each. Hanover heads the text 'The Ascent of Mount Ventoux, Francis Petrarch, Familiar Letters. From James Harvey Robinson, ed. and trans., Petrarch: The First Modern Scholar and Man of Letters (New York: G.P. Putnam, 1898)', addresses it 'To Dionisio da Borgo San Sepolcro', marks the span 307-320 and puts [Page 308] inside the first sentence, between 'which is not improperly called' and 'Ventosum'; Fordham carries the same break as (308). So the translator, the year, the page span and the claim that these are the opening sentences all check out, and Familiares IV.1 is the standard number for this letter. Nothing here is minted: the wording is Robinson's own, public domain, and the same in two independent transcriptions. Attribution is uncontested and absent from the misattribution list; shipped.js returns no match, no near match, Petrarch at 0 of 3, not banned; the tag Correspondence is the form of the work; scope, publishability and the theme are all sound, and 'My only motive was the wish to see what so great an elevation had to offer' is April's own line about setting out. Two things for the note rather than the citation. The letter's dateline is Malaucene, April 26 (1336 by tradition), but scholarship since Billanovich holds it was composed years later and may be a literary construction rather than the report of a day's climb; the source line asserts no date, so nothing false ships, and a note that said 'the letter dates itself 26 April' would be the honest wording. And the shipped locator would be stronger with the recipient in it, since 'opening sentences' alone does not identify which letter of the Familiares; betterCitation adds him and still fits 140 characters at 133.
